overview: Prominent themes were section 82 notices on withheld information, the status of 2022 Auditor General amendment legislation, and the office's independence and funding. Members repeatedly cited Management of Housing Maintenance Information, the Progress of the Infant, Child and Adolescent Mental Health System Transformation Program audit and WA's progress on the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations, alongside Public Accounts Committee reviews, the Rail Freight, Westport and State Development bills, and Estimates Division 12.

issues.label: Section 82 notices on withheld information
issues.note: Members pressed ministers to table notices under section 82 of the Financial Management Act so the Auditor-General can report on whether refusals were reasonable.

issues.label: Auditor-General independence, legislation and funding
issues.note: Members debated the status of 2022 Auditor General amendment legislation, WA's independence ranking, the office's budget increase and its access to documents.

issues.label: Mental health transformation program audit
issues.note: The June 2026 audit of the infant, child and adolescent mental health transformation prompted questions and debate; the government said it accepts all recommendations.

issues.label: Child safe organisations audit
issues.note: Members quoted the November 2025 report finding WA lagging other jurisdictions on legislation mandating the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations.

issues.label: Public housing maintenance audit
issues.note: Members cited the August 2025 Management of Housing Maintenance Information report on vacant property work orders, reactive maintenance and contractor audit coverage.

issues.label: Parliamentary committees and audit follow-up
issues.note: The Public Accounts Committee considered 23 Auditor-General reports and followed up nine, including the Perth Parking Levy; estimates committee consultation also featured.

debates.gist: Public Accounts Committee's annual report tabled. Speakers described its review of Auditor-General reports and wished the Auditor-General well; the deputy chair opposed proclaiming earlier amendment legislation, and a third member cited the Perth Parking Levy follow-up.

Members cited the Auditor-General's August 2025 findings on vacant property work orders and contract audits in a motion on public housing waitlists and vacant homes; one speaker said the Greens rejected linking migration to the waitlist.

Debate on the Estimates and Financial Operations Committee's report. Members noted its consultation with the Auditor-General, including a 17 September hearing on local government audit fees, and one said Western Australia gets the balance right between committees and Auditors-General.

Second reading of the rail freight acquisition bill. Members cited Auditor-General statements on the old lease's value, network maintenance and disclosure to Parliament; one sought an independent review with an Auditor-General role, and another argued separate legislation reduced the Auditor-General's accountability.

Motion on essential services. Members cited the Auditor-General on health payments (weak controls, fraud risk), the water regulator's inability to confirm lawful extraction, and the Geraldton health precinct as an overdue, over-budget project.

Question time on the Auditor-General's report, tabled that day, on the infant, child and adolescent mental health transformation. One member asked whether the Minister for Mental Health agreed with its findings and another whether the minister had sought a status report on all 32 taskforce recommendations; the minister said the government accepts all recommendations.

Estimates hearing for the Office of the Auditor General. Questions covered section 82 notifications processed, a fall in Western Australia's independence ranking among Auditors-General, access to cabinet documents and a 1.6% funding rise; the Auditor-General began to mention a potential topic list.

Second reading of the Treasurer's advance bill. One member said the unassented Auditor General Amendment Bill 2022 signals weaker scrutiny; another relied on audited results with an Auditor-General opinion for past net debt; a third quoted the major IT projects report on cost overruns.

Debate on the Gold Corporation Amendment Bill. The Auditor-General featured through the bill's retention of Financial Management Act and Auditor General Act coverage, and a question on whether the Auditor-General would still receive an unredacted copy when commercially sensitive material is removed.

Committee-stage questions on the State Development Bill. The Auditor-General appeared in an interjection on annual report timeframes, an answer that the office reports on statutory timeframes, and a claim that it shares the view that the water rights law is inadequate.

Second reading and committee stage of the State Development Bill. Members cited Auditor-General audits finding weak water licence and ecological community protection, asked about integrity engagement with the Auditor-General, and quoted a letter on the 2024 state agreements review.

Motion on infrastructure delivery. Members cited the Auditor-General on Geraldton Health Campus as the most delayed major project, a $205 million gap between budgeted and actual vehicle licence fees for local roads, and public housing maintenance costs and reactive spending.

Motion on the gender diversity service model of care that turned to government transparency. Members cited the Auditor-General on transparency and on about half of section 82 decisions being not reasonable; a government member said the office's funding has more than doubled.

WA-0001.summary: Said the Auditor-General, in forming an opinion on the 2025–26 Annual Report on State Finances, reviews the accounting assessment of native title claims and the contingent liability assessments included in the report.

WA-0002.summary: Tabled the Public Accounts Committee's annual report, saying it considered 23 Auditor-General reports and followed up nine in Review of Selected Auditor General Reports 2022–2024, and wished the Auditor-General a good recovery.

WA-0003.summary: Said a notice of motion aims to stop proclamation of a bill the member called draconian and claimed would water down the Auditor-General's transparency; also praised the committee's work, wished the Auditor-General well and urged members to attend the briefing.

WA-0004.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's February 2023 findings on Perth Parking Levy administration and said the committee's follow-up found the transport department had made no progress on the five recommendations; the levy held an estimated $194 million.

WA-0005.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's findings in Management of Housing Maintenance Information in a public housing motion: only 51% of vacant property work orders met the 14-day target, and there is no clear end-to-end measure of how long homes sit empty.

WA-0006.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's August 2025 finding that just over half of vacant property work orders met the 14-day target, alongside answers showing 107 vacant public homes in Kalgoorlie as of June 2026.

WA-0007.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report that Housing and Works audits 5.7% of work orders and only 1.62% of audits are physical inspections, and argued extending head maintenance contracts to June 2028 delays the fix.

WA-0008.summary: Said the Greens support parts of the motion but reject linking migration to the public housing waitlist; the Auditor-General appears only in an interjection describing the content of the earlier speech.

WA-0009.summary: Urged members to read what the Auditor-General has said on housing maintenance, quoting the motion's reference to 51% of vacant work orders meeting the target, and asked whether anything has changed since the August 2025 report.

WA-0010.summary: Asked whether the Mental Health Commission has now set baseline measures to assess the Infant, Child and Adolescent Mental Health System Transformation Program, citing the Auditor-General's finding that it failed to complete the required baseline assessment.

WA-0011.summary: Said, for the Minister for Mental Health, that the Mental Health Commission has accepted the Office of the Auditor-General's report recommendations, is progressing actions, and remains on track to complete them within the timeframe the office provided.

WA-0012.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's October 2023 report on the Road Trauma Trust Account, which identified shortcomings in expenditure priorities, assessment of funding applications and evaluation of outcomes, and argued transparency matters as camera revenue rises.

WA-0013.summary: Said the committee consults the Auditor-General through regular dialogue as its terms of reference require, and argued Western Australia gets the balance right between parliamentary committees and Auditors-General, remarking on the difficulty of the Tasmanian role.

WA-0014.summary: Described the committee's 17 September hearing with the Auditor-General on local government audit fees and recalled, as a former shire councillor, being sceptical of the 2017 audit change and asking whether the office audited departments such as Communities.

WA-0015.summary: Noted the committee report's reference to consultation with the Auditor-General, including a hearing on 17 September 2025 and an earlier hearing with office staff on 11 September 2024, while reviewing the report.

WA-0016.summary: Mentioned in passing that the committee consults regularly with the Auditor-General, as its report says, while speaking about the budget estimates process.

WA-0017.summary: Gave notice of a motion to condemn the government over legislation the motion says undermines the Auditor-General's independence, and to call for a halt to proclaiming the remaining Auditor General Act 2022 provisions and for amending legislation.

WA-0018.summary: Asked whether it is normal for a bill to include a clause on what information the Auditor-General may disclose, and urged the government not to proclaim the pending Auditor General Act changes, which the member argued remove transparency.

WA-0019.summary: Said the unproclaimed bill gave the Auditor-General rights over cabinet documents but the Auditor-General does not want it, and explained the rail bill's clause lets the Auditor-General respond to consultation requests, such as on past Public Transport Authority accounts.

WA-0020.summary: Asked the minister to provide information lawfully available to the Legislative Council or else comply with section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006 so the Auditor-General can report on whether the decision is reasonable and appropriate.

WA-0021.summary: Asked the Treasurer to provide the information requested or comply with section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006 so the Auditor-General can report on whether the decision is reasonable and appropriate.

WA-0022.summary: Asked whether a matter might fall within the Office of the Auditor-General's purview or another entity's, and was told the Auditor-General has an auditing and oversight role over the Office of State Revenue's activities.

WA-0023.summary: Said the Auditor-General has an auditing and oversight role over the Office of State Revenue's activities, the Corruption and Crime Commission could oversee misconduct allegations, and Parliament can call agencies before committees.

WA-0024.summary: Read from a 2004 report a member's dissent that an oversight mechanism was already in place, since standing orders had the Legislative Council's Public Administration and Finance Committee consult regularly with officers including the Auditor General, and noted members differed on the question then.

WA-0025.summary: Questioned why the proposed joint committee would oversee five office holders but not the Public Sector Commissioner or the Auditor-General, saying there is little clarity on why some were chosen and others left out.

WA-0026.summary: Said the bill's reforms respond to concerns raised by local governments and the Office of the Auditor-General, describing the aim as a modern, effective and sustainable local government sector.

WA-0027.summary: Cited the Auditor-General as saying there was no evidence of the $400 million track upgrade promised when the rail network was leased, and that the lease and its variations had not been tabled in Parliament.

WA-0028.summary: Cited a 2013 Auditor-General report on managing the rail freight network as finding many original objectives of the lease had been achieved, including lower costs and debt paydown, with the lease and freight business sale providing $588 million.

WA-0029.summary: Mentioned in passing that, under standing orders, the estimates committee consults with the Auditor-General on the state's financial administration, while describing the committee's functions and its 94th report.

WA-0030.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report Payments to Subcontractors Working on State Government Construction Projects, which found three entities administered PBAs without due scepticism and with little checking of head contractors' information, and argued scepticism is central to review work.

WA-0031.summary: Asked the minister to table the requested documents or else comply with section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006 so the Auditor-General can report on whether the decision is reasonable and appropriate.

WA-0032.summary: Said the Auditor-General and a parliamentary inquiry raised concerns about rail network maintenance and information given to Parliament, and argued that experience bears on clause 29, which lets commercially sensitive information be removed from published material.

WA-0033.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's 2012 finding that the rail freight network's replacement cost had passed $5 billion, set against a $292 million lease, and said the Auditor-General sounded warnings years ago, with grain lines since degrading.

WA-0034.summary: Called for an independent review of the rail freight transaction's governance and compliance with a role for the Auditor-General, saying a review after the event cannot replace proper controls before the agreement is signed.

WA-0035.summary: Argued that a bill still awaiting royal assent has reduced the Auditor-General's accountability and transparency, and described the rail bill as asking Parliament to write a blank cheque on trust.

WA-0036.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report this year of a lack of progress in transforming infant, child and adolescent mental health services, while noting care and response teams exist but are only for acute situations.

WA-0037.summary: Asked the Attorney General to comply with section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006 by tabling and giving the Auditor-General written notice of a decision to withhold MOU information, so the Auditor-General can report on whether it was reasonable.

WA-0038.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's review of state agreement projects as finding that a range of matters should count towards a state agreement's total value, and argued value is not just about collecting the most royalties.

WA-0039.summary: Mentioned the Auditor-General in passing, urging that advice from reports, including the Auditor-General's, be taken up and reasonable questions answered, while speaking about support for children and young people.

WA-0040.summary: Asked the Attorney General to table the review's report, due nearly six months earlier, or comply with section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006 so the Auditor-General can give an opinion on withholding it.

WA-0041.summary: Said the Auditor-General is among the usual checks on the new authority, which would face performance and specific audits and the same duty to give the Auditor-General information as other agencies, and answered concerns about its Procurement Act exemption.

WA-0042.summary: Asked what the authority would be subject to under the Auditor General Act, was told it faces the same obligations as other agencies, and asked whether the bill or regulations would interfere with the Act's or the Financial Management Act's application.

WA-0043.summary: Asked the minister to table a version of the report, and why written notice had not been given to Parliament and the Auditor-General within 14 days as section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006 requires.

WA-0044.summary: Tabled the committee's 2025–26 activity report, noting a September 2025 hearing with the Office of the Auditor-General on local government financial audit fees and the committee's observation that the Auditor-General is making a concerted effort to consult local governments.

WA-0045.summary: Described the bill's structure for the new authority, noting it would sit outside the public sector management framework while remaining subject to the Financial Management Act and the Auditor General Act.

WA-0046.summary: Asked the minister whether and when the notice required under section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006 would be tabled, so the Auditor-General can give an opinion on whether the refusal was reasonable and appropriate.

WA-0047.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's latest report on nearly $1 billion in health payments, which the member said found weak controls, payments without adequate evidence, procurement failures and elevated fraud risk, and argued the government is not in control of Health.

WA-0048.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's 2025 report as stating the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation is not doing enough to protect water resources and does not know if water is extracted legally, and argued the department is under-resourced.

WA-0049.summary: Said the Auditor-General once described the Geraldton health precinct as the most overdue and over-budget project on the government books, while welcoming the new emergency department and mental health unit.

WA-0050.summary: Argued that providing current valuations of land to be exchanged under the Lot 551 agreement with Burswood Nominees to the Auditor-General before the agreement is finalised is a simple measure fitting integrity and probity.

WA-0051.summary: Mentioned the Auditor-General in passing, alongside the Corruption and Crime Commissioner and the Commissioner for Children and Young People, as examples of independent oversight, while arguing animal wellbeing lacks comparable independence.

WA-0052.summary: Said the Auditor-General identified concerns in 2014 and again in 2019, and argued there was no shortage of warnings, as a national database recommended 11 years ago is only now being delivered.

WA-0053.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report WA's Progress to Implement the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations as shedding light on government progress, which the member said paints a grim picture, after no public progress reports since 2022.

WA-0054.summary: Asked, citing the Auditor-General's report Progress of the Infant, Child and Adolescent Mental Health System Transformation Program, when the current implementation working group was established.

WA-0055.summary: Asked, in light of the Auditor-General's report on the Infant, Child and Adolescent Mental Health System Transformation Program, why the ministerial oversight committee's implementation working group ceased to exist in January 2023.

WA-0056.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's performance audit Progress of the Infant, Child and Adolescent Mental Health System Transformation Program, handed down four years after the taskforce's final report with 32 accepted recommendations, and noted $235 million put into the program.

WA-0057.summary: Said the government has accepted all the Auditor-General's recommendations on the Infant, Child and Adolescent System Transformation Program and is putting in place strengthened governance arrangements to provide assurance about their implementation.

WA-0058.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's finding that government agencies did not use or know of the mental health implementation plan, and argued only one recommendation had been implemented more than three years into a transformation meant to take five years.

WA-0059.summary: Said the government accepts the Auditor-General's recommendations on the infant, child and adolescent mental health report, argued the report recognised new and expanded services delivering positive outcomes, and said implementation will continue with renewed focus.

WA-0060.summary: Tabled the Public Accounts Committee's fourth report, Review of selected Auditor General Reports 2022–2024, summarising its consideration of 23 Auditor-General reports and follow-up of nine, with state entity responses on implementing recommendations published in the appendixes.

WA-0061.summary: Spoke as Deputy Chair on the tabling of Review of selected Auditor General Reports 2022–2024, saying the committee's work ensures public money is spent appropriately, and thanked the Auditor-General for ensuring transparency for taxpayers.

WA-0062.summary: Said the select committee's report recommends that updated independent valuations be publicly released and the agreement independently reviewed by the Auditor-General before being finalised, noting no current independent valuation has been released.

WA-0063.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's performance audit of progress on the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations, quoting findings that Western Australia is lagging other jurisdictions and, nearly eight years on, still lacks legislation mandating compliance with the principles.

WA-0064.summary: Said successive governments have not disclosed amounts committed to major events for commercial reasons, and that the Auditor-General has supported this approach on several occasions, including four during the previous government's term.

WA-0065.summary: Asked when the minister first became aware that the Western Australia Police Force could provide a rudimentary cost estimate, citing the Auditor-General's report 18 of 2025–26 on the cost of supervising, monitoring and transporting a person on bail during trial.

WA-0066.summary: Asked the Minister for Mental Health whether the minister agrees with the Auditor-General's report, tabled that day, as described by the member: that the Mental Health Commission has no credible plan and unaddressed gaps would stop the reforms being delivered as intended.

WA-0067.summary: Said the government welcomes the Auditor-General's report and accepts its recommendations in full, citing the report as highlighting new and expanded services, and said $235 million has been invested in infant, child and adolescent mental health since 2022.

WA-0068.summary: Asked, referring to the Auditor-General's report tabled that afternoon on mental health reform implementation, whether the minister had asked the Mental Health Commissioner for a status report on all 32 taskforce recommendations and, if not, why not.

WA-0069.summary: Opened a question by referring to the November 2024 Office of the Auditor-General report on the Aboriginal Procurement Policy and Australian National University work on companies eligible for the federal Indigenous Procurement Program.

WA-0070.summary: Said, answering a question on the power to declare a place a venue, that it would go through a cabinet process and the usual oversight applies, including the Auditor-General, cabinet and Treasurer, plus public scrutiny.

WA-0071.summary: Said the trust's Knutsford land valuation was updated after the Auditor-General found the Landgate valuation did not demonstrate fair market value, that trustees adopted an independent $26.85 million valuation, and that no impropriety was found.

WA-0072.summary: Asked the minister to explain how the trust's holdings came to be valued at $39.9 million, said to derive from an Office of the Auditor-General report, against the original $19 million valuation.

WA-0073.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's record that the government declined to provide information on the Griffin Coal Ashurst engagement, so the refusals could not be assessed, and argued commercial-in-confidence claims obstruct scrutiny; urged members to attend Auditor-General meetings.

WA-0074.summary: Read out a colleague's question referring to the 2009 and 2016 Auditor-General reports on the Main Roads maintenance backlog, each quoting about $800 million, as an example of frustration with a minister's answer.

WA-0075.summary: Said the government has more than doubled the Office of the Auditor-General's budget, from $24.1 million in 2016–17 to $53 million in 2024–25, describing it as an investment in accountability and transparency.

WA-0076.summary: Said an approach to the environment would take note of national state of the environment reports and Office of the Auditor-General assessments, then resource conservation and environmental regulation; the Auditor-General is mentioned briefly.

WA-0077.summary: Said Mr Whitby refused to tell Parliament what an operation cost and is the subject of an Auditor-General investigation under a section 82 notice, and looked forward to the opinion on whether that was reasonable and appropriate.

WA-0078.summary: Cited a 2024 Auditor-General report as somewhat critical of state agreement management and finding little public information, and asked what the department has done in two years to make the agreements publicly available, such as on a website.

WA-0079.summary: Said the 2024 Auditor-General report was an important audit and that the department did extensive internal work beforehand on foundations, technology and capability to administer state agreements and maximise their benefits.

WA-0080.summary: Estimates committee heading for Division 12, Office of the Auditor General, listing the chair, the Treasurer and the Office of the Auditor-General staff appearing, including the Auditor-General and Acting Deputy Auditor-General.

WA-0081.summary: Asked how many section 82 notifications were processed in 2024–25 and this year to date. The Treasurer referred the question to the Auditor-General, who said two in 2025 and one in progress in 2025–26.

WA-0082.summary: When asked the reasons for WA's fall from third to sixth in an independence ranking of Auditors-General, referred the question to the Auditor-General. When later pressed for an undertaking on independence, said cabinet document access now exists and further change would be considered but is not a priority.

WA-0083.summary: Started to refer to portfolios identified in the office's potential topic list before the Chair interrupted; the excerpt does not show the answer.

WA-0084.summary: Mentioned the Auditor-General in passing, noting the committee still wanted to get to that division, before asking how many loans have been established under various Keystart home loan products.

WA-0085.summary: Mentioned the Office of the Auditor-General in passing, asking to end questioning on the Western Australian Treasury Corporation out of respect for the office.

WA-0086.summary: Asked whether recommendations from an Office of the Auditor-General report on Greenough, tabled over 12 months earlier, had been implemented, which were outstanding and why the government had taken time to act.

WA-0087.summary: Asked which report the member meant, the Auditor-General's or the Inspector of Custodial Services', and was told it concerned the women's unit at Greenough and had about 12 recommendations.

WA-0088.summary: Said the agency reviewed its effectiveness and efficiency indicators, with some advice from the Office of the Auditor-General, so the measures better reflect its performance.

WA-0089.summary: Asked whether recommendations from an Auditor-General report on information systems had been implemented; the answer given was that the Assist replacement is ongoing and the office lifted its qualification in September 2025.

WA-0090.summary: Said the Assist replacement program is ongoing, the department has reviewed the Office of the Auditor-General's report and recommendations, and the office lifted its qualification in September 2025 after the department addressed concerns in its opinion.

WA-0091.summary: Said the member had insisted a more recent Auditor-General valuation put the fund at nearly $40 million when the government described about $20 million, and argued the government now cites $40 million after downplaying it.

WA-0092.summary: Argued land worth hundreds of millions of dollars was moved to DevelopmentWA without a proper accounting mechanism, citing past Auditor-General comments on land transferred between agencies without proper accounting, and questioned DevelopmentWA's value.

WA-0093.summary: Asked the Treasurer whether and when the Treasurer will comply with section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006 and give notice of the decision so the Auditor-General can publish an opinion on whether it was reasonable and appropriate.

WA-0094.summary: Argued that audited financial reports carrying the Auditor-General's approval show the debt under the previous government, and criticised the Treasurer's spokesman for relying on older forecasts, which the member called misleading.

WA-0095.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Financial Audit Results Local Government 2025 as highlighting severe pressure on local government financial sustainability from operating losses, declining cash reserves and compliance burden, and argued state cost shifting is behind the decline.

WA-0096.summary: Asked the minister whether and when the minister will comply with section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006 and give notice of the decision so the Auditor-General can publish an opinion on whether it was reasonable and appropriate.

WA-0097.summary: Said the Auditor-General once described Geraldton Health Campus as the government's most delayed and over-budget project, and argued another $3 million is being added, taking the cost beyond $190 million almost a decade on.

WA-0098.summary: Said the Office of the Auditor-General focused years ago on criticism that funds were used on poorly specified, unevaluated projects, and that the member has not seen the full outcome of governance improvements, though money now appears freed up for its purpose.

WA-0099.summary: Responded to concerns raised in the Auditor-General's 2022 performance audit, saying the three audited agencies have since improved but reliance on head contractors' statutory declarations alone falls short, and that audited entities committed to and implemented recommendations.

WA-0100.summary: Described the Legislative Council's motion as alleging the Treasurer failed to progress the Auditor-General's recommendations on special purpose accounts for the Perth parking levy, leaving concerns about purpose, consultation, transparency, reporting and a spending plan.

WA-0101.summary: Quoted a statement that local governments need sufficient time to meet Local Government Act 1995 obligations and Auditor-General guidelines on budget amendments for borrowings, and asked the minister why the bill sets 28 days.

WA-0102.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's 2022 findings, which the member called damning: weak controls on subcontractor payments, statutory declarations accepted without due scepticism, reliance on subcontractor complaints and no proactive spot checks.

WA-0103.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Management of Housing Maintenance Information report, tabled August 2025, saying 85% of the 240,000 maintenance jobs examined were reactive and so costly, in an argument about a waitlist rising 56% since 2019.

WA-0104.summary: Compared tenure models for independent officers, noting the Auditor-General serves a single 10-year term without reappointment, and said the benefit of such a model is that no structural deficiency weakens the Commissioner for Children and Young People's voice.

WA-0105.summary: Motion text alleging, among other matters, that the Treasurer failed to progress the Auditor-General's recommendations on the Perth parking levy special purpose account, leaving concerns about purpose, consultation, transparency and reporting.

WA-0106.summary: Moved a motion alleging, among other matters, that the Treasurer failed to progress the Auditor-General's recommendations on the Perth parking levy special purpose account, leaving concerns about purpose, consultation, transparency and reporting.

WA-0107.summary: Said the Auditor-General's 2022–23 report Administration of the Perth Parking Levy identified issues but the government introduced 2023 legislation to modernise the Perth Parking Management Act 1999 and levy administration, and argued the motion fails to acknowledge that response.

WA-0108.summary: Moved an amendment to a notice of motion alleging, among other matters, that the Treasurer failed to progress the Auditor-General's recommendations on the Perth parking levy special purpose account, leaving concerns about transparency and reporting.

WA-0109.summary: Argued the Auditor General Amendment Bill 2022, passed by both houses but still without royal assent four years on, leaves the Auditor-General in legislative ambiguity and, with the advance's scale and budget structure, signals a weaker scrutiny environment.

WA-0110.summary: Argued that audited whole-of-government results carrying an Auditor-General opinion, not older forecasts, should be used to state past net debt, reading the 2016–17 figure from them, and said the Treasurer used discredited numbers instead.

WA-0111.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's 2025 Transparency Report: Major IT Projects, saying projects were about $1 billion over cost and half had estimated costs at least doubled, and claimed police agreed to cost controls that were not put in place.

WA-0112.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's recent transparency report as confirming the Geraldton Health Campus upgrade is the most delayed major project in Western Australia, almost five years late, with completion now not expected until 2027.

WA-0113.summary: Said the committee's report records 15 refusals to answer questions, which section 82 of the Financial Management Act requires to be reported to Parliament and the Auditor-General, and claimed none of the notices was appropriately tabled.

WA-0114.summary: Claimed the unassented Auditor General Amendment Bill 2022 restricts the Auditor-General's access to documents, argued the government will not explain how a $1.6 billion advance is spent, and asked about the Auditor-General's assessment of the Geraldton emergency department.

WA-0115.summary: Noted that the GTE act's financial administration and audit provisions will not apply to Gold Corporation, which remains subject to the Financial Management Act 2006 and Auditor General Act under section 54 of the Gold Corporation Act.

WA-0116.summary: Said Gold Corporation will remain subject to the Financial Management Act and Auditor General Act for oversight, and when asked whether the Auditor-General would get an unredacted copy, said that turns on document access, which would probably be unfettered.

WA-0117.summary: Asked whether a full unredacted copy would still be made available to the Auditor-General, separate from deleting a commercially sensitive element, and was told it depends on the Auditor General Act's document access, thought to be generally unfettered.

WA-0118.summary: Asked how many section 82 notices the minister tabled in 2025, whether the minister received any reminder letters from the Auditor-General about that obligation, and, if so, whether the letters would be tabled.

WA-0119.summary: Said existing checks and balances on procurement include legislation and integrity agencies such as the Public Sector Commission, the Office of the Auditor-General and the Corruption and Crime Commission, and argued there is plenty of scrutiny and transparency.

WA-0120.summary: Asked the minister to comply with section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006 by giving the Auditor-General notice of the decision, and asked when the department's health policy was last and will next be reviewed.

WA-0121.summary: Explained that section 82 of the Financial Management Act requires a minister's refusal to provide information to be formally reported to Parliament and the Auditor-General so the refusal can be scrutinised, as the committee's report outlines.

WA-0122.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's finding that hundreds of patients waiting for aged-care or disability services spent around 40,000 extra days in hospital after being medically ready for discharge, an average of more than 80 days each.

WA-0123.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report on progress implementing the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations, quoting findings that Western Australia lags other jurisdictions and lacks mandating legislation, and noted the Ombudsman was announced as oversight body during the audit.

WA-0124.summary: Cited the Office of the Auditor-General's report tabled last November, saying its foreword is stark and critical of a lack of delivery by the government and the Department of Communities.

WA-0125.summary: Said basic questions should receive basic answers and that the member would prefer not to write to the Auditor-General about a section 82 matter or lodge a freedom of information request.

WA-0126.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's 27 November report WA's Progress to Implement the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations, which described the government's slow progress on royal commission recommendations as disappointing, and rejected any suggestion the opposition is at fault.

WA-0127.summary: Cited two Auditor-General reports: on public housing, which the member said found maintenance and information tracking poor with 85% of maintenance reactive, and on threatened ecological communities being ineffectively monitored and protected.

WA-0128.summary: Said the Auditor-General's report on major projects found the Geraldton hospital redevelopment was the most delayed of all the major hospital projects, while welcoming that a hospital will finally serve the Mid-West.

WA-0129.summary: Discussed the 90-day timeframe for annual reports; the Auditor-General is mentioned only in an interjection that reports containing finances, which the Auditor-General works on, must be tabled within that time.

WA-0130.summary: Said a ministerial direction can require an authority to comply with a timeframe notice, and that compliance with statutory timeframes is also reported on by the Auditor-General.

WA-0131.summary: Argued the Rights in Water and Irrigation Act is outdated and fails to regulate water adequately, saying this is not only the member's view but also that of the Office of the Auditor-General.

WA-0132.summary: Asked whether the minister recalls telling the house that the minister would write to both houses and the Auditor-General under section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006, and whether the minister knows this must happen within 14 days.

WA-0133.summary: Cited Office of the Auditor-General findings that the water regulator does not effectively monitor or enforce conditions on over 12,000 licences and the biodiversity department is not fully protecting 65 ecological communities, arguing the bill speeds approvals without a functioning compliance framework.

WA-0134.summary: Asked what work the government did with the Corruption and Crime Commission or the Auditor-General on the integrity and corruption-risk implications of the bill's broad discretions, and was pointed to the Public Sector Commission's principles of conduct.

WA-0135.summary: Said the bill does not deal with post-approval auditing or the Auditor-General's requirements and that the Auditor-General's report on other approvals processes falls outside the clause 1 debate, when asked about two reports on environmental compliance.

WA-0136.summary: Quoted a letter saying the bill does not incorporate the recommendations of the Auditor-General's 2024 review of state agreements, which noted that special laws lack transparency about social and community benefits, and linked this to earlier critiques of the bill.

WA-0137.summary: Gave notice of a motion alleging, among other matters, that the Treasurer failed to progress the Auditor-General's recommendations on the Perth parking levy special purpose account, leaving concerns about purpose, consultation, transparency and reporting.

WA-0138.summary: Asked whether the minister considers it reasonable and appropriate not to provide the information to Parliament and, if so, whether the minister will notify both houses and the Auditor-General as section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006 requires.

WA-0139.summary: Included the Auditor-General's performance audit report tabled on 27 November, which the member called damning, among the matters supporting a motion on the government's response to sexual abuse.

WA-0140.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report, which the member called very damning, saying 310 of 400 recommendations relate to Western Australian Government actions with many yet to be implemented, and that WA and the Northern Territory alone lack legislation for the National Principles.

WA-0141.summary: Asked whether the Auditor-General's 2024 review of state agreements, which noted that special laws lack transparency about social and community benefits, was taken on board in drafting the bill, and suggested a committee could explore it.

WA-0142.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report WA's Progress to Implement the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations, saying it raised serious concerns about progress, particularly the Department of Communities, and quoting that WA lags other jurisdictions and still lacks mandating legislation.

WA-0143.summary: Cited a 2023 Auditor-General report as naming the Geraldton Health Campus expansion the most delayed major project, within a speech on regional health infrastructure waits of up to nine years and lack of local cancer services.

WA-0144.summary: Cited an Office of the Auditor-General audit of vehicle licence fee funding for the local government road network, which the member said found a $205 million disparity between budgeted and actual fees from 2014 to 2024.

WA-0145.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report on public housing maintenance, which the member said found costs up 44% since 2019 while activity rose 7% and 85% of maintenance was reactive, and said the department spent $256 million on travel and overheads.

WA-0146.summary: Asked for the current dollar value of the Main Roads maintenance backlog as defined in the Auditor-General's 2009 and 2016 reports, which put it at $820 million and $845 million respectively.

WA-0147.summary: Said part 4 of the bill lets the minister issue directions and ensures full compliance with the Financial Management Act and Auditor General Act, keeping the trust accountable to Parliament while retaining commercial flexibility.

WA-0148.summary: Asked whether the minister is aware WA is one of two jurisdictions without legislation mandating the National Principles, and whether anyone is being held accountable for the fragmented approach and missing implementation plan the Auditor-General found.

WA-0149.summary: Relayed advice from the Department of Communities that the minister acknowledges the Office of the Auditor-General's report on implementing the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations; the excerpt ends before further detail.

WA-0150.summary: Argued the bill lacks robust independent oversight, including mandatory engagement with the Environmental Protection Authority and with the Auditor-General as the integrity body for each use of modification orders.

WA-0151.summary: Asked, citing the Auditor-General's housing maintenance report, how much would be recouped if 50% of work orders were audited rather than 5.7%, the length and annual value of the Programmed Facility Management contract, and the amount overcharged in 2024–25.

WA-0152.summary: Said the Auditor-General's report showed the housing stock the state owns and delays in simple maintenance of vacant properties before they can be occupied again, and argued the state government has a part to play.

WA-0153.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report this year as finding the government does not know the condition of most of its regional housing stock, including Government Regional Officers' Housing, with only 19% of properties having an up-to-date condition assessment.

WA-0154.summary: Opened a question citing the Auditor-General's 24th report PathWest's Laboratory Information System, which found major weaknesses in managing confidentiality and integrity of blood and tissue test result information; the excerpt ends before the questions.

WA-0155.summary: Said the Western Australia Police Force is unable to provide a cost due to its operational nature, and that under section 82 of the Financial Management Act 2006 the minister will write to both houses and the Auditor-General in due course.

WA-0156.summary: Cited an Office of the Auditor-General report on the shire's finances, saying it found mismanagement, poor governance, material uncertainty about going concern and liabilities exceeding assets by more than $14.2 million for the year ending 30 June 2024, plus improper dismissals.

WA-0157.summary: Said 8% of the Shire of Beverley's budget goes to the Auditor-General for audit fees, which the member called ridiculous for a budget of roughly eight million dollars, as an example of regulatory burden on regional local governments.

WA-0158.summary: Asked whether the dollar figure requested for the Main Roads overdue maintenance backlog, as defined in the Auditor-General's 2009 and 2016 reports, exists, noting no data was provided in answer to the earlier question.

WA-0159.summary: Tabled the Public Accounts Committee's annual report, noting two meetings with the Auditor-General, four reports tabled including Review of selected Auditor General reports 2019–2024, and follow-up on implementation of audit recommendations.

WA-0160.summary: Argued the government lacks transparency, asked what the Auditor-General has said about such matters, and claimed it is unprecedented for an Auditor-General to have to keep raising a government's lack of transparency.

WA-0161.summary: Said the government has more than doubled the Office of the Auditor-General's funding, from $24.1 million to $53.8 million, and cited the Langoulant report that until 2016–17 the Auditor-General ruled over 40% of ministerial decisions to withhold information unjustified.

WA-0162.summary: Said ministers have issued section 82 notices 39 times since taking office, compared with 55 in an earlier premier's second term, and cited the Auditor-General's finding that about half such decisions were not reasonable and therefore not appropriate.

WA-0163.summary: Said the government's lack of transparency is common knowledge and that even the Auditor-General says so, in responding to an earlier speaker's explanation of the timing of a document's release.

WA-0164.summary: Asked for the latest assessed dollar value and length of road in the Main Roads maintenance backlog, using the Auditor-General's 2009 and 2016 definition (about $800 million), after an earlier answer gave only a $22 million carryover.
